question: In a DC generator, the EMF actually induced in each armature coil is:

options.text: Alternating, and it is converted to DC by diodes in the field winding
Direct, so the commutator only serves to carry the current out of the rotating armature
Alternating, and it is converted into a unidirectional output by the commutator and brushes
Direct, and the commutator smooths out its ripple

explanation: A coil rotating in a field always produces an alternating EMF. The commutator — a split ring of segments — reverses each coil's connection to the brushes at the moment its EMF reverses, so the brushes always see the same polarity.

question: The output voltage of a DC generator depends on:

options.text: Its speed of rotation and the strength of its field flux
Its speed of rotation only, since the field is fixed
The load current only, since voltage rises with load in every generator
The field flux only, since speed has no effect on induced EMF

explanation: Induced EMF is proportional to the rate at which the armature conductors cut flux — so to both speed and flux. Engine speed varies widely, so voltage is held constant by adjusting the flux through the field current.

question: Most aircraft DC generators are shunt-wound. In a shunt-wound generator the field winding is:

options.text: Connected in series with the armature, so it carries the full load current
Supplied from a separate permanent magnet machine, never from the armature
In parallel with the armature, with its current varied to control voltage
Connected in series with the load, after the reverse current cut-out

explanation: A shunt field carries only a small current and its strength can be varied independently of load, which makes voltage regulation straightforward. A series generator's voltage rises with load, which makes it unsuitable for supplying a busbar.

question: As engine speed increases, the voltage regulator of a DC generator keeps the output voltage constant by:

options.text: Increasing the current in the field winding, so the flux is stronger
Inserting resistance in series with the armature output
Disconnecting the generator from the bus until the speed falls again
Reducing the current in the field winding, so the flux is weaker

explanation: A faster armature would produce more EMF from the same flux. The regulator compensates by cutting field current. At low speed it does the opposite, up to the point where full field current is not enough — below that speed the generator cannot maintain bus voltage.

question: A carbon pile voltage regulator varies the field current of a generator by:

options.text: Changing the number of turns in the field winding through a selector
Varying the pressure, and so the resistance, of a carbon disc stack in the field circuit
Varying the speed of the generator through a constant speed drive
Switching the field current on and off thousands of times per second with transistors

explanation: A spring compresses the carbon stack, lowering its resistance; an electromagnet sensing generator voltage opposes the spring. If voltage rises, the electromagnet relieves the pressure, resistance rises and field current falls. Modern regulators do the same job electronically.

question: The reverse current cut-out (RCCO) of a DC generator closes to connect the generator to the bus when:

options.text: The engine is started, whatever the generator voltage
The generator voltage just exceeds the bus voltage
The generator voltage falls below the battery voltage
The load current exceeds the generator's rated output

explanation: Connecting a generator with a lower voltage than the bus would make it draw current. The cut-out therefore waits until generator voltage exceeds bus voltage, so that current flows outward from the start.

question: If there were no reverse current cut-out and the engine-driven DC generator slowed down below its cut-in speed:

options.text: The generator would continue to charge the battery at a reduced rate
Nothing would happen, since current cannot flow into a generator
The generator voltage would rise to compensate for the lower speed
The battery would discharge into the generator, trying to drive it as a motor

explanation: A DC machine is reversible. With its EMF below the battery's, current would flow from the battery into the armature, discharging the battery and possibly damaging the generator. The RCCO senses that reverse current and disconnects the generator.

question: A light-aircraft alternator system does not need a reverse current cut-out because:

options.text: Its rectifier diodes stop current flowing back into it from the battery
The battery switch disconnects it automatically when the engine stops
Its voltage is always higher than the battery's, whatever the engine speed
Its field is a permanent magnet, so it cannot be motored

explanation: The output of an alternator passes through its rectifier bridge. A diode will not conduct in reverse, so when alternator output falls below battery voltage, no current flows back — the diodes do the cut-out's job.

question: In a typical light-aircraft alternator, the field winding:

options.text: Is a permanent magnet, so no field current is ever needed
Is on the stator, and the output is taken from the rotor through a commutator
Is on the rotor, fed via slip rings, with the output from fixed stator windings
Is in series with the output, so it carries the full load current

explanation: Putting the small field current through slip rings and taking the large output from stationary windings avoids a commutator carrying heavy current. The stator's three-phase AC is rectified to DC by diodes inside the alternator.

question: A light aircraft with a completely flat battery is hand-swung and the engine starts. The alternator will most likely:

options.text: Run as a motor and stall the engine
Fail to produce output, because its field needs battery voltage to be excited
Produce excessive voltage, because there is no battery load to regulate against
Produce normal output and recharge the battery straight away

explanation: Unlike a self-excited DC generator with residual magnetism, most aircraft alternators rely on the battery to energise their rotor field. With no battery voltage there is no field and no output. This is one reason a dead battery should be investigated, not simply bypassed.

question: An advantage of an alternator over a DC generator in a light aircraft is that the alternator:

options.text: Needs no voltage regulator, because its output is fixed by its design
Can give useful output at low engine speeds and is lighter for its output
Can recharge a completely flat battery without external help
Produces DC directly, with no need for rectification

explanation: Alternators are lighter, need no heavy commutator and, with a suitable pulley ratio, can charge even at idle — a DC generator often cannot. They still need a regulator, still need the battery to excite the field, and still rectify AC internally.

question: If a generator's voltage regulator fails so that full field current is applied, the overvoltage protection will:

options.text: Reduce engine speed automatically to lower the generator output
Trip the generator off line by removing its field excitation
Increase the load on the generator until the voltage falls back
Connect the battery in parallel to absorb the excess voltage

explanation: A runaway regulator can drive the output far above normal, burning out lamps and avionics and boiling the battery. The overvoltage relay senses this and removes excitation (and usually opens the generator line contactor), leaving the battery to supply the bus.

question: Two DC generators are operating in parallel. Load sharing between them is achieved by:

options.text: Fixing both engines at exactly the same rpm throughout the flight
Connecting both field windings in series across the battery
An equalising circuit that trims each generator's field excitation
Inserting a fixed resistor in each generator's output line

explanation: Even a small voltage difference makes the higher-voltage generator take most of the load. An equalising (load-sharing) loop compares the generators' currents and trims each regulator, raising the field of the lightly loaded one and lowering that of the heavily loaded one.

question: Two paralleled DC generators are poorly matched: one supplies 90% of the load and the other only 10%. The most likely cause is that:

options.text: Their output frequencies are different
Their regulated output voltages are slightly different
One of their reverse current cut-outs has opened
They are rotating in opposite directions

explanation: Because generator internal resistance is very low, a fraction of a volt difference produces a large difference in current. DC machines have no frequency to match; an opened cut-out would put the whole load on the other generator.

question: A starter-generator, as used on many turboprops and small jets, is:

options.text: One DC machine that motors the engine to start, then generates
A battery charger that also powers the starter solenoid
A generator with a separate starter motor sharing the same drive shaft
An AC generator that is started by a small DC motor on its end

explanation: Using one machine for both jobs saves weight. During the start it is supplied from the battery or ground power (often with a series winding for high torque); once the engine is self-sustaining it switches to generating, controlled by a regulator and a line contactor.

question: The brushes of a DC generator or motor are usually made of carbon because carbon:

options.text: Has the lowest resistance of any conducting material available
Is non-magnetic and so does not disturb the main field
Prevents any sparking at the commutator under all conditions
Is self-lubricating and wears instead of the copper commutator

explanation: A softer, self-lubricating carbon brush rides on the commutator with little wear to the expensive copper segments, and the brushes themselves are the replaceable part. Brush wear increases in very dry air at altitude, an early problem for high-flying DC aircraft.

question: Armature reaction in a DC generator refers to:

options.text: The voltage drop across the brushes at high load
The mechanical vibration of the armature at high rotational speed
Distortion of the main field by the armature current's own field
The reverse current that flows when the generator is motored

explanation: The current in the armature conductors creates its own field, which twists the main field and shifts the neutral plane, causing sparking at the brushes. Interpoles or compensating windings, carrying the load current, are fitted to cancel it.

question: 'Flashing the field' of a DC generator means:

options.text: Briefly feeding the field from the battery to restore residual magnetism
Momentarily short-circuiting the output to test the reverse current cut-out
Switching the field on and off rapidly to regulate the output voltage
Applying a high voltage to the armature to clean the commutator

explanation: A self-excited generator needs residual magnetism in its poles to start building voltage. If it has been lost (by heat, shock or reverse polarity), a short pulse of current from the battery in the correct polarity restores it.

question: Why is the regulated voltage of a 24 V aircraft system set at about 28 V?

options.text: Because 28 V is the voltage at which the reverse current cut-out opens
To compensate for the voltage drop in the battery's internal resistance during engine start
So that the battery supplies part of the load in normal flight
So the generator voltage exceeds the battery's and keeps it charged

explanation: Charging requires the source voltage to exceed the battery's EMF. A nominal 24 V battery charges correctly at about 28 V, so systems are called '28 V DC' — the same reasoning gives 14 V for a 12 V light-aircraft system.

question: In a light aircraft, the alternator (or generator) warning light illuminates in flight. This indicates that:

options.text: The alternator is supplying more than its rated current
The battery is being overcharged and the alternator should be switched off
The battery is fully charged and the alternator has stopped charging it
The alternator has stopped supplying the bus; the battery carries the load

explanation: The light typically comes on when alternator output falls below bus voltage. From then on the battery alone supplies everything, and its endurance is limited — the time to reduce load and plan a landing.

question: A DC generator is called a self-excited machine when:

options.text: Its field is provided by permanent magnets, with no winding
It is driven by its own electric motor rather than by the engine
Its field winding is supplied from its own armature output
Its field winding is supplied from a separate battery at all times

explanation: Self-excitation means the generator feeds its own field. A separately excited machine takes field current from an outside source. Most aircraft DC generators are self-excited shunt machines that rely on residual magnetism to begin building up.

question: A series-wound DC generator is unsuitable for supplying an aircraft busbar because:

options.text: Its voltage rises with load current, so it cannot hold the bus steady
It cannot produce any output until it is fully loaded
Its field winding carries no current, so it has no means of excitation
Its output is alternating rather than direct current

explanation: In a series machine the whole load current passes through the field. More load means a stronger field and a higher voltage — the opposite of what a constant-voltage bus needs, and a reason the field winding of a series generator cannot be regulated independently of load.

question: The output of a light-aircraft alternator is regulated by:

options.text: A voltage regulator controlling the rotor field current
A constant speed drive between the engine and the alternator
A rheostat in series with the three-phase stator output
The rectifier diodes, which block any voltage above 14 V

explanation: As with a DC generator, the output depends on speed and field strength, and the regulator controls the field current. The diodes only rectify; they have nothing to do with regulating the voltage.

question: In a light aircraft, a sudden large positive reading on the ammeter accompanied by flickering, very bright lights most likely indicates:

options.text: An overvoltage condition caused by a failed voltage regulator
Failure of the alternator, with the battery taking the load
A normal recharge of the battery after engine start
A short circuit in the landing light, which has lowered the bus voltage

explanation: A regulator stuck at full field drives the alternator voltage well above normal: the battery is charged hard (high ammeter reading) and lamps burn brightly. If an overvoltage relay is fitted it should trip the alternator; otherwise the alternator side of the master switch is turned off.

question: The EMF induced in a generator's armature can be increased by:

options.text: Moving the conductors parallel to the lines of flux
Increasing the resistance of the armature winding
Turning it slower, so each conductor stays longer in the field
Turning it faster, using a stronger field, or adding more turns

explanation: The induced EMF depends on how fast flux is cut: more speed, more flux density, or more turns cutting it all raise the voltage. Moving parallel to the flux cuts none at all.
